dryRun.title: Mark and sweep
rows: start from globals, the current call stack, active closures
follow every reference, mark each object reached
free every object that was not marked
object still in a Map / listener / timer
dryRun.note: JavaScript frees memory automatically: anything unreachable from the roots is garbage, even objects that point at each other. A "leak" means something you no longer need is still reachable.

think.q: let a = {}; let b = { a }; a.b = b; a = b = null. Can the two objects be freed?
why: Reference counting could not free cycles; modern engines use reachability, which can.

think.q:
let cache = new Map()
let user = { name: 'A' }
cache.set('u', user)
user = null
console.log(cache.get('u').name)
why: Setting the variable to null removes one reference, but the Map still holds the object, so it stays reachable (and alive).

think.q:
function make() { const big = new Array(3).fill('x'); return () => big.length }
const f = make()
console.log(f())
why: The closure keeps big reachable as long as f exists.

think.q: When does garbage collection run?
opts: When the engine decides, usually under memory pressure; you cannot trigger it from normal code
Only when you set a variable to null
why: You control reachability, not timing.

think.q: Which tool shows what keeps an object alive in Chrome?
opts: A heap snapshot in DevTools → Memory, with its "retainers" view
why: Take a snapshot, filter by class name, and read the retainer path back to a root.

try.task: Write reachable(roots): given root objects whose references are listed in a refs array property, return a Set of every object reachable from the roots (mark phase). It must handle cycles.
examples: const a = { refs: [] }, b = { refs: [a] }; a.refs.push(b); reachable([a]).size  // 2
try.hint: A stack (or queue) of objects to visit and a Set of seen ones; skip objects already seen.

checks.verify: const c = { refs: [] }, b = { refs: [c] }, a = { refs: [b] }; const s = reachable([a]); assert(s instanceof Set && s.has(c) && s.size === 3, "chain")
const a = { refs: [] }, b = { refs: [a] }; a.refs.push(b); assert(reachable([a]).size === 2, "cycle")
const lost = { refs: [] }, a = { refs: [] }; const s = reachable([a]); assert(s.has(a) && !s.has(lost), "unreachable")

takeaway.key: Unreachable = freed, cycles included. A leak is an object you no longer need that is still reachable.
mistakes: Thinking x = null frees an object that is still referenced elsewhere.
Trying to control when GC runs.

dryRun.title: Map vs WeakMap holding data about a DOM node
dryRun.note: WeakMap/WeakSet hold their keys weakly: the entry does not keep the key alive. Perfect for metadata, caches and private data per object. WeakRef holds a single object weakly, and FinalizationRegistry lets you know (eventually) when it was collected.

think.q:
const wm = new WeakMap()
try { wm.set('key', 1) } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) }
why: Weak keys must be objects (or non-registered symbols). Strings can never be collected, so they are not allowed.
think.exec:
const wm = new WeakMap()
try { wm.set('key', 1) } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) }

think.q:
const ws = new WeakSet()
const o = {}
ws.add(o)
console.log(ws.has(o), typeof ws.size, typeof ws[Symbol.iterator])
why: Weak collections have no size and are not iterable: their contents can change at any time due to GC.

think.q:
const ref = new WeakRef({ v: 1 })
console.log(ref.deref()?.v)
why: deref() returns the object if it has not been collected yet. Right after creation it is still there; later it might be undefined.
think.exec:
const ref = new WeakRef({ v: 1 })
console.log(ref.deref()?.v)

think.q:
const priv = new WeakMap()
class User { constructor(n) { priv.set(this, { n }) } get name() { return priv.get(this).n } }
const u = new User('A')
console.log(u.name, Object.keys(u).length)
why: WeakMap private data: invisible on the instance and freed with it. (Today #private fields do the same more simply.)

think.q: You cache the computed layout for each DOM element. Which structure?
why: The cache entry should disappear when the element is gone.

try.task: Write memoizeByObject(fn): cache fn(obj) per object argument in a WeakMap, so cached results disappear with the object. Return the memoized function.
examples: const f = memoizeByObject((o) => o.x * 2); const o = { x: 2 }; f(o); f(o)  // fn ran once
f({ x: 2 })  // a new object: runs again

checks.verify: let n = 0; const f = memoizeByObject((o) => (n++, o.x)); const o = { x: 1 }; f(o); f(o); assert(f(o) === 1 && n === 1, "cache")
let n = 0; const f = memoizeByObject((o) => (n++, o.x)); f({ x: 1 }); f({ x: 1 }); assert(n === 2, "identity")

const f = memoizeByObject((x) => x); assert(typeof f === "function", "must return a function"); let t = false; try { f("str") } catch (e) { t = e instanceof TypeError }; assert(t, "should throw TypeError")

takeaway.key: WeakMap/WeakSet keys do not keep objects alive: use them for per-object metadata and caches. They are not iterable and have no size.
mistakes: Using a Map for per-element data and leaking detached elements.
Expecting WeakRef.deref() to always return the object.

dryRun.title: The usual suspects
rows: the element/window holds the handler, which holds its closure
the timer list holds the callback
a global Map keeps every entry
detached DOM node in a variable
your variable still points at it
dryRun.note: A leak is memory that grows because things you no longer need stay reachable. In UIs the classic cases are listeners and timers that outlive the component that created them.

think.q:
const handlers = []
function mount() { const big = new Array(1000).fill(0); handlers.push(() => big.length) }
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) mount()
console.log(handlers.length)
why: Each mount adds a handler that captures its own big array, and nothing ever removes them.

think.q:
const ac = new AbortController()
const target = new EventTarget()
let n = 0
target.addEventListener('ping', () => n++, { signal: ac.signal })
target.dispatchEvent(new Event('ping'))
ac.abort()
target.dispatchEvent(new Event('ping'))
console.log(n)
why: Aborting the signal removes every listener registered with it. One abort cleans up many listeners.
think.exec:
const ac = new AbortController()
const target = new EventTarget()
let n = 0
target.addEventListener('ping', () => n++, { signal: ac.signal })
target.dispatchEvent(new Event('ping'))
ac.abort()
target.dispatchEvent(new Event('ping'))
console.log(n)

think.q:
let ticks = 0
const id = setInterval(() => { ticks++; if (ticks === 3) clearInterval(id) }, 1)
setTimeout(() => console.log(ticks), 50)
why: clearInterval stops the timer and releases its callback. Without it the callback runs (and stays alive) forever.

think.q:
const cache = new Map()
function get(k) { if (!cache.has(k)) cache.set(k, k * 2); return cache.get(k) }
for (let i = 0; i < 10000; i++) get(i)
console.log(cache.size)
why: An unbounded cache keyed by ever-new values grows without limit. Cap it (LRU) or key it weakly.

think.q: How do you confirm a leak in a page?
opts: Look for errors in the console
Repeat the action (open/close the dialog) several times and compare heap snapshots: memory keeps growing
why: A leak shows as growth that never comes back after GC.

try.task: Write lruCache(limit) returning { get(k), set(k, v), size } that keeps at most limit entries, evicting the least recently used. get counts as a use. (size is a getter.)
examples: const c = lruCache(2); c.set("a", 1); c.set("b", 2); c.get("a"); c.set("c", 3)  // "b" is evicted
try.hint: A Map keeps insertion order: on get, delete and re-set the key; on set over the limit, delete map.keys().next().value.

checks.verify: const c = lruCache(2); for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) c.set(i, i); assert(c.size === 2 && c.get(99) === 99 && c.get(0) === undefined, "limit")
const c = lruCache(2); c.set("a", 1); c.set("b", 2); c.get("a"); c.set("c", 3); assert(c.get("a") === 1 && c.get("b") === undefined && c.get("c") === 3, "lru")

checks.t: setting an existing key updates it
checks.verify: const c = lruCache(2); c.set("a", 1); c.set("a", 5); assert(c.get("a") === 5 && c.size === 1, "update")

takeaway.key: Leaks are things that stay reachable: listeners, timers, caches, detached nodes, big closures. Clean up on unmount; bound your caches.
mistakes: Adding listeners or intervals in a component without removing them.

dryRun.title: Eager vs lazy: first 2 even squares of 1…1,000,000
dryRun.note: Lazy evaluation computes a value only when it is needed. Generators make lazy pipelines; getters and memoized functions make lazy properties. It pays off for big or infinite sequences and expensive values that may never be used.

think.q:
let work = 0
function* nums() { for (let i = 1; ; i++) { work++; yield i } }
function* map(it, f) { for (const x of it) yield f(x) }
function* take(it, n) { if (n <= 0) return; for (const x of it) { yield x; if (--n === 0) return } }
console.log([...take(map(nums(), (x) => x * x), 3)].join(), work)
why: Only 3 values are pulled through the pipeline, so only 3 are produced, even from an infinite source.

think.q:
let calls = 0
const cfg = { get heavy() { calls++; return 42 } }
console.log(calls, cfg.heavy, cfg.heavy, calls)
why: A getter is lazy but recomputes on every read. Cache it if it is expensive.

think.q:
let calls = 0
const cfg = { get heavy() { calls++; Object.defineProperty(this, 'heavy', { value: 42 }); return 42 } }
cfg.heavy; cfg.heavy
console.log(calls)
why: The getter replaces itself with a plain value on first read: lazy and computed once.
think.exec:
let calls = 0
const cfg = { get heavy() { calls++; Object.defineProperty(this, 'heavy', { value: 42 }); return 42 } }
cfg.heavy; cfg.heavy
console.log(calls)

think.q:
const a = [1, 2, 3, 4]
let checks = 0
const hit = a.find((x) => (checks++, x > 1))
console.log(hit, checks)
why: find, some and every stop early, so they do not check the rest.
think.exec:
const a = [1, 2, 3, 4]
let checks = 0
const hit = a.find((x) => (checks++, x > 1))
console.log(hit, checks)

think.q: When is lazy evaluation a bad idea?
opts: When the value is needed anyway and computing it later happens at a worse moment (e.g. during a click)
why: Laziness moves the cost; it does not remove it.

try.task: Write a lazy helper lazy(iterable) returning an object with chainable map(f), filter(f), take(n) and a final toArray(). Nothing may be computed before toArray, and it must work on an infinite generator.
try.hint: Store a generator-producing function; each method wraps it in a new generator and returns lazy(newIterable).

checks.verify: function* nat() { for (let i = 1; ; i++) yield i } assert(JSON.stringify(lazy(nat()).map((x) => x * x).take(3).toArray()) === "[1,4,9]", "infinite")
let n = 0; const chain = lazy([1, 2, 3]).map((x) => (n++, x)); assert(n === 0 && chain.toArray().length === 3 && n === 3, "eager")

takeaway.key: Compute only what is used: generator pipelines for sequences, self-replacing getters or memoization for expensive values.
mistakes: Building huge intermediate arrays to use two items.
Lazy getters that recompute an expensive value on every read.

dryRun.title: Events at 0, 50, 100, 150, 400 ms, wait = 200
dryRun.note: Debounce: run once after things go quiet (search box, resize end, autosave). Throttle: run at most once per interval while things keep happening (scroll position, mousemove, rate-limited buttons).

think.q: Live search: call the API when the user pauses typing. Which?
why: You want one call after the burst, not a steady stream during it.

think.q: Update a "scrolled %" bar smoothly while the user scrolls. Which?
why: Debounce would freeze the bar until scrolling stops.

think.q:
function debounce(fn, ms) { let t; return (...a) => { clearTimeout(t); t = setTimeout(() => fn(...a), ms) } }
const log = []
const d = debounce((x) => log.push(x), 20)
d(1); d(2); d(3)
setTimeout(() => console.log(log.join()), 60)
why: Each call cancels the previous timer; only the last call runs, with its arguments.

think.q:
function throttle(fn, ms) { let last = -Infinity; return (...a) => { const now = Date.now(); if (now - last >= ms) { last = now; fn(...a) } } }
const log = []
const t = throttle((x) => log.push(x), 1000)
t(1); t(2); t(3)
console.log(log.join())
why: The first call runs; the rest within 1000 ms are dropped. (A trailing throttle would also run the last one later.)

think.q: In a React component, const onChange = debounce(save, 300) is written in the body. Typing saves on every key. Why?
opts: debounce does not work in React
A new debounced function (with a new timer) is created on every render
why: Create it once (useMemo/useRef) so all calls share one timer.

try.task: Implement debounce(fn, ms) with a .cancel() method and throttle(fn, ms) (leading edge: the first call runs immediately, then at most once per ms). Both pass the latest arguments.
examples: const d = debounce(save, 300); d("a"); d("b")  // save("b") once, 300 ms later
const t = throttle(track, 100); t(); t(); t()  // track runs once
try.hint: debounce: clearTimeout + setTimeout in a closure. throttle: remember the last run time.

checks.t: debounce runs once with the last arguments
checks.verify: const got = []; const d = debounce((x) => got.push(x), 20); d(1); d(2); d(3); await sleep(50); assert(got.join() === "3", got.join())
const got = []; const d = debounce((x) => got.push(x), 20); d(1); d.cancel(); await sleep(40); assert(got.length === 0, "cancel")

checks.t: throttle runs the first call and drops the burst
checks.verify: const got = []; const t = throttle((x) => got.push(x), 50); t(1); t(2); t(3); await sleep(60); t(4); assert(got.join() === "1,4", got.join())

takeaway.key: Debounce = once after the burst; throttle = at most once per interval during it. Create them once, not on every render.
mistakes: Using debounce for things that must update during the activity.
Re-creating the debounced function each render.

dryRun.title: Main thread vs worker
rows: a separate script on another thread
heavy CPU work: parsing, image processing, crypto
dryRun.note: A Web Worker runs JavaScript on another thread so heavy work does not freeze the page. There is no shared memory by default: messages are copied with the structured clone algorithm (or ArrayBuffers are transferred, leaving the sender with an empty buffer).

think.q:
const original = { d: new Date(0), m: new Map([[1, 2]]), nested: { a: [1] } }
const copy = structuredClone(original)
copy.nested.a.push(2)
console.log(original.nested.a.length, copy.m.get(1), copy.d instanceof Date)
why: postMessage uses structured clone: a deep copy that keeps Dates and Maps. Changes on one side do not affect the other.

think.q: try { structuredClone({ f() {} }) } catch (e) { console.log(e.name) }
why: Functions cannot be cloned, so you cannot send them to a worker. Send data, not behaviour.

think.q:
const buf = new ArrayBuffer(8)
const moved = structuredClone(buf, { transfer: [buf] })
console.log(buf.byteLength, moved.byteLength)
why: Transferring moves the buffer instead of copying: fast for big data, and the sender can no longer use it.

think.q: Which task is the best fit for a Web Worker?
why: Workers help with long CPU work. They have no DOM, and messaging has a cost.

think.q: Inside a worker, which is NOT available?
why: Workers have no DOM. They do have timers, fetch and messaging.

try.task: Without a worker, keep the page responsive: write processInChunks(items, chunkSize, fn) that calls fn on each item, but yields to the event loop (with setTimeout) after every chunk. Resolve with the array of results.
examples: // a timer scheduled before it can run between chunks
try.hint: Loop over slices; after each slice await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r)).

checks.verify: const r = await processInChunks([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2, (x) => x * 2); assert(JSON.stringify(r) === "[2,4,6,8,10]", JSON.stringify(r))

let ran = false, seenAt = -1, i = 0; setTimeout(() => { ran = true; seenAt = i }); await processInChunks([1, 2, 3, 4], 1, () => i++); assert(ran && seenAt > 0 && seenAt < 4, "did not yield: " + seenAt)
const r = await processInChunks([], 3, (x) => x); assert(Array.isArray(r) && r.length === 0, "empty")

takeaway.key: Workers move heavy CPU work off the main thread; messages are deep-copied (structured clone) or transferred. No DOM inside.
mistakes: Sending functions or DOM nodes to a worker.
Using a worker for tiny tasks where messaging costs more than the work.
